overview: Adidas AG is a German sporting goods company that designs, develops, produces (via third-party contract manufacturers), and markets athletic and lifestyle footwear, apparel, and accessories under the adidas brand. The company operates globally through seven reportable geographic segments (Europe, North America, Greater China, Latin America, Emerging Markets, and the combined Japan/South Korea), selling through wholesale partners, owned retail stores, and e-commerce. Adidas is the world's second-largest sportswear company by revenue, behind Nike, and is in the third year of a brand and operational turnaround led by CEO Bjørn Gulden.

business_model.summary: Adidas earns revenue by designing and marketing footwear, apparel, and accessories that are manufactured by third-party contract factories (primarily in Vietnam, Indonesia, China, and Cambodia) and sold through wholesale retail partners and the company's own direct-to-consumer (DTC) channels (own retail stores and e-commerce). Revenue is largely transactional/seasonal (product-cycle driven, tied to sell-in and sell-through of footwear/apparel collections) rather than subscription-based, though strong franchise momentum (e.g., Samba/Gazelle 'Terrace' lifestyle shoes) and licensed team/athlete partnerships provide some repeat-purchase durability. FY2025 group net sales were €24,811 million, up 5% reported (+13% currency-neutral) with operating profit of €2,056 million (8.3% operating margin), both up sharply from FY2024 (€23,683m sales, €1,337m operating profit, 5.6% margin), reflecting post-Yeezy and turnaround-driven margin recovery.
business_model.customer_type: B2C (end consumers via wholesale partners, own retail, and e-commerce) with B2B wholesale relationships with large sporting goods retailers, department stores, and sports federations/clubs/athletes as marketing partners
business_model.geographic_mix: Europe ~33% of FY2025 net sales (€8,136m), North America ~20% (€5,087m), Greater China ~15% (€3,623m), Emerging Markets ~14% (€3,510m), Latin America ~12% (€2,926m), Japan/South Korea ~6% (€1,406m). All regions posted double-digit currency-neutral growth in FY2025 except North America (which still grew double digits in Q3 2025). Channel mix for FY2025: wholesale +12% currency-neutral, own retail +13%, e-commerce +16%, combined DTC +14%.

competitive_position.market_position: Clear #2 global sportswear brand behind Nike, and gaining share: Nike's estimated global share slipped to roughly 12.7% in 2025 (down ~1.5pp) while Adidas posted record 2025 revenue and two consecutive years of double-digit currency-neutral growth. In the UK, Euromonitor data cited by analysts shows Nike at ~21% retail value share vs. adidas at ~16% and Puma at ~4%, with adidas continuing to take share from Nike. Adidas has also reclaimed category credibility in football (market leadership) and running at the high end.

moat_factors.description: 76-year-old global brand with deep roots in both performance sport and streetwear/lifestyle culture; the Three Stripes, Originals, and Terrace franchises (Samba, Gazelle, Spezial, Superstar) carry outsized cultural cachet, reinforced by celebrity/athlete collaborations (Bad Bunny, Pharrell, Wales Bonner) and Ballon d'Or-winning athletes.

Large, diversified third-party manufacturing base (Vietnam ~39% of footwear, plus Indonesia, China, Cambodia) gives cost leverage versus smaller rivals, though it also concentrates tariff/geopolitical exposure.

Long-term partnerships with major football clubs (Liverpool FC, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich, Manchester United), national federations (DFB), and athletes create marketing moat and halo effects (e.g., 2026 World Cup jersey sales) difficult for smaller challenger brands to replicate.
Extensive wholesale shelf space plus a growing owned retail/e-commerce fleet provide broad consumer access, though wholesale remains exposed to retailer inventory and discounting cycles.

Decentralized regional go-to-market strategy under Gulden (e.g., China pet-collection launch, market-specific product ranges) has driven simultaneous double-digit growth across virtually all regions, a differentiator versus more centrally-managed competitors.

weaknesses: Reliance on retro/lifestyle 'Terrace' footwear franchises (Samba/Gazelle) that are showing signs of fading popularity/fashion-cycle risk, per Reuters commentary in late 2025
Lower barriers to entry in sneakers have let challenger brands (On, Hoka, Li Ning, Anta) erode share from incumbents including both Nike and Adidas
No strong structural moat equivalent to network effects or switching costs — consumer loyalty is brand/fashion-driven and can rotate quickly
North America remains the weakest major region relative to Europe/China/Latin America growth rates
Heavy dependence on a small number of large contract manufacturers and geographies (Vietnam/Indonesia) for footwear production

growth_drivers: Continued 'Terrace' lifestyle franchise momentum (Samba, Gazelle, Spezial, relaunched Superstar) and expansion into new silhouettes (SL72, Samba Jane/Mule) and apparel extensions of heritage footwear lines

Performance category credibility rebuild — football market leadership regained, Running franchise (Adizero, Evo SL, Supernova) delivering marathon wins and >30% growth in Q3 2025, Basketball innovation

Greater China recovery — double-digit currency-neutral growth for multiple consecutive years, regaining share lost during the 2021-2022 boycott-driven downturn, while Nike's China business has been declining
Major 2026 sporting events calendar (Winter Olympics, FIFA World Cup — adidas sold ~18 million World Cup-related jerseys in Q2 2026) driving marketing halo and apparel/performance sales
DTC and e-commerce mix shift (e-commerce +16% in FY2025) supporting full-price realization and gross margin expansion
Margin recovery as one-off Yeezy-related costs fully roll off (last Yeezy inventory sold by end of 2024) and operating leverage improves via SG&A discipline
Potential US tariff refunds (~€200m booked in Q3 2026, with CEO citing potential for ~€300m total following a US Supreme Court-related ruling) as a tailwind to reported profit
Medium-term targets: ~€2 billion of incremental annual revenue in both 2027 and 2028, with an ambition to reach double-digit operating margin

business.description: Samba/Gazelle-driven lifestyle demand shows signs of normalizing/fading per late-2025 reporting; the Terrace cycle cannot be assumed to continue indefinitely, and industry-wide excess inventory/discounting in lifestyle footwear was flagged by CEO Gulden in Q3 2026.

On Holding, Hoka, New Balance, Li Ning, and Anta-owned brands are taking share; Barclays forecasts sector growth of only ~4%/year 2026-2029 (ex-Nike ~6%), implying a more competitive, lower-growth backdrop than the historical duopoly era.
Much of the turnaround narrative is attributed directly to CEO Bjørn Gulden's strategy and personal credibility with retailers and athletes; succession or departure risk is a consideration.

business.risk: Wholesale partner concentration and retailer bargaining power
business.description: Retailers control shelf space allocation; Adidas management has noted it does not yet have the shelf space it believes it deserves in all categories/markets.

financial.description: A strengthening euro reduced FY2025 and Q3 2025 reported revenue growth by over €1 billion/€300 million respectively versus currency-neutral growth; most sales are generated outside the eurozone.
Hyperinflation-related effects caused significant swings in net financial result/net income in Q3 2025 despite strong operating performance.

Average operating working capital rose to 23.0% of net sales in FY2025 (above the updated 21-22% target) as inventories grew 17% to support growth, consuming cash — operating cash flow fell sharply to €751 million in FY2025 from €2,910 million in FY2024.

regulatory.description: US reciprocal tariffs on Vietnam (~20%) and Indonesia/Philippines (~19%) as of mid-2025, with earlier rates far higher (46%/32%), directly raise landed costs on footwear; management flagged a potential $218-231 million 2025 cost impact and an estimated ~€400 million combined tariff/FX drag on FY2026 operating profit, partially offset by refunds.

regulatory.risk: EU sustainability/ESRS and supply-chain due-diligence regulation
regulatory.description: Adidas now reports a full ESRS-compliant Sustainability Statement with limited assurance, reflecting rising compliance costs under EU CSRD and supply-chain (forced labor, environmental) due-diligence rules.
CEO has cited a pending US Supreme Court-related tariff ruling as the basis for a potential ~€300 million duties refund; outcomes remain uncertain and the benefit (unlike the cost) is not guaranteed.

macro.description: Footwear/apparel purchases are discretionary; a global consumer slowdown would pressure both wholesale sell-through and DTC traffic.
Greater China remains ~15% of sales; past geopolitical/boycott episodes (2021 Xinjiang cotton controversy) show the China business can swing sharply; ongoing US-China trade tensions are a tail risk.
Product and freight costs are a direct driver of gross margin; FY2025 margin gains were partly attributed to lower product/freight costs, which could reverse.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global sportswear industry growth is expected to moderate to roughly 4% per year for 2026-2029 (about 6% excluding Nike, per Barclays), as the historical Nike-Adidas duopoly erodes and challenger brands (On, Hoka, Li Ning, Anta) gain share. Big 2026 sporting events (Winter Olympics, FIFA World Cup) provide a cyclical tailwind.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate — footwear/apparel is a discretionary consumer category with product/fashion cycles (e.g., lifestyle 'Terrace' demand) layered on top of macro consumer spending cycles; major sporting events create periodic demand spikes.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low-moderate direct sensitivity (manageable leverage, adjusted net borrowings/EBITDA of 1.4x at FY2025), moderate indirect sensitivity via consumer discretionary spending and working-capital financing costs.
key_input_costs: Contract manufacturing labor costs (Vietnam, Indonesia, China, Cambodia)
US import tariffs on finished goods

recent_developments.event: Record quarterly revenue of €6.63 billion (adidas brand +12% currency-neutral), operating profit up 23% to €736 million (11.1% margin); FY2025 outlook raised to ~9% currency-neutral revenue growth and ~€2.0 billion operating profit (from €1.7-1.8bn).

Net sales of €24,811 million (+5% reported, +13% currency-neutral, second consecutive year of double-digit growth), operating profit €2,056 million (8.3% margin, vs 5.6% in FY2024), net income attributable to shareholders up 75% to €1,340 million; dividend raised 40% to €2.80/share.

2026 outlook of high-single-digit currency-neutral sales growth and operating profit of around €2.3 billion, with management flagging an estimated ~€400 million combined tariff/FX drag concentrated in H1 2026.
Q1 2026 earnings beat expectations on continued strong demand; management reiterated confidence despite tariff/FX headwinds.

Operating profit rose only 5% to €574 million, below consensus of ~€620 million, pressured by World Cup-related marketing spend; shares fell on the miss. Management nonetheless raised FY2026 currency-neutral revenue growth guidance to 9-10% (from high-single-digit) while holding the ~€2.3 billion operating profit target (excluding any tariff refunds). Adidas sold ~18 million World Cup-related jerseys; apparel revenue +35%, performance-category sales +39% in the quarter.

Record quarterly operating profit above €1.0 billion (+37%) on revenue of €7.252 billion (+9% reported, +7% currency-neutral), gross margin up 2.5pp to 54.3%, aided by a ~€200 million US tariff refund; FY2026 operating profit guidance raised to ~€2.5 billion (potentially up to €2.6 billion), with revenue growth guidance maintained at 9-10% currency-neutral. Shares rose ~3%. CEO Gulden flagged industry-wide excess inventory/discounting pressure in lifestyle footwear and said Samba/Gazelle popularity is gradually normalizing.

CEO Gulden stated adidas would likely be entitled to further US tariff duty refunds (cited a potential ~€300 million figure) following a favorable US Supreme Court-related trade ruling; Citigroup flagged Adidas, Puma, and H&M as key beneficiaries of broader tariff-refund dynamics across the sector.

items.vs_prior: raised (from high-single-digit at FY2025 results, then raised to 9-10% at Q2 2026, maintained at Q3 2026)
items.notes: Driven by broad-based regional and channel growth plus 2026 World Cup/Winter Olympics tailwinds

items.vs_prior: raised (from ~€2.3 billion guided at FY2025 results and maintained through Q2 2026)
items.notes: Includes a ~€200 million US tariff refund booked in Q3 2026; management flagged plans to reinvest ~€100 million into Q4 marketing/operational initiatives; excludes any additional future tariff refunds not yet recognized

items.metric: Average operating working capital (% of net sales)
items.vs_prior: raised versus FY2025's 21-22% target range, reflecting FY2025 actual of 23.0%
items.notes: Inventory growth (+17% in FY2025) to support demand has pushed working capital intensity above prior targets

items.vs_prior: lowered versus FY2025's ~€600 million target (FY2025 actual: €477 million)

items.notes: Part of medium-term targets set out in 2023 turnaround plan; also targeting double-digit operating margin over the medium term

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Bjørn Gulden described 2025 as a success, citing 14% brand growth and EBIT margin above 10% for the first nine months, and said the 'global potential for adidas is almost unlimited.' Entering 2026, he flagged the Winter Olympics and the largest-ever FIFA World Cup as growth catalysts, while cautioning about a volatile tariff and consumer environment. At Q3 2026, Gulden acknowledged industry-wide inventory/discounting pressure in lifestyle footwear and gradually fading Samba/Gazelle demand, while emphasizing continued strength in Performance categories (Running, Football) and broad-based regional growth.

bull_case: Three-year turnaround under CEO Bjørn Gulden has driven two consecutive years of double-digit currency-neutral revenue growth and a sharp operating margin recovery (5.6% in FY2024 to 8.3% in FY2025, tracking toward double digits), with FY2026 operating profit guidance raised twice already to ~€2.5bn
Regained credibility and market leadership in performance categories (football) and strong momentum in running (Adizero marathon wins), reducing reliance on fading lifestyle/retro trends
Greater China has returned to sustained double-digit growth even as Nike's China business has been shrinking, suggesting Adidas is winning share in one of the industry's most important growth markets
2026 sporting calendar (Winter Olympics, FIFA World Cup) provides a multi-quarter demand and marketing tailwind, evidenced by ~18 million World Cup jerseys sold and 35-39% category growth in Q2 2026
Potential upside from US tariff refund litigation (already booked ~€200m, with management citing further ~€300m potential), a cash tailwind not available to all competitors to the same degree
bear_case: Lifestyle/Terrace franchise momentum (Samba, Gazelle) that powered much of the turnaround is showing signs of fading per CEO's own Q3 2026 commentary, with industry-wide inventory and discounting pressure building in lifestyle footwear

Structurally slower industry growth expected (~4%/year 2026-2029 per Barclays) as On, Hoka, New Balance, Li Ning, and Anta-owned brands erode the historical Nike-Adidas duopoly, challenging adidas's own medium-term 'high-single-digit' growth ambitions

Heavy exposure to US tariffs on Vietnam/Indonesia-made goods creates ongoing cost and guidance uncertainty; refund benefits are not guaranteed and FY2026 guidance explicitly excludes any unbooked future refunds

Rising working capital intensity (23.0% of sales in FY2025, above target, driven by 17% inventory growth) has sharply reduced operating cash flow (down from €2,910m to €751m in FY2025), raising questions about the quality/sustainability of reported earnings growth

Valuation already reflects much of the turnaround optimism (shares up strongly from 2023 lows before a 2026 pullback), leaving less room for error if event-driven 2026 tailwinds (World Cup, Olympics) prove temporary rather than durable share gains
